Series::logaddexp¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::logaddexp(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::logaddexp_(const Series& other)

What It Does¶

logaddexp() computes log(exp(a) + exp(b)) elementwise, where a is the receiver and b is other.

Written that way it looks trivial, but the naive spelling is a trap. If a is 1000, then exp(a) is about 2e434, which overflows float64 to inf, and the whole expression collapses to inf even though the true answer is close to 1000.

logaddexp() is the numerically stable version. It factors out the larger operand:

m = max(a, b)
result = m + log(exp(a - m) + exp(b - m))
       = m + log1p(exp(-|a - b|))

Now both shifted exponents are <= 0, so exp of them is in (0, 1] and cannot overflow. The log1p form (log(1 + x) computed accurately for small x) also keeps precision when a and b are far apart.

This operation is the heart of working in log-space: it is how you add two probabilities that are stored as log-probabilities without leaving log-space. logaddexp() is the two-argument, broadcasting form; a full log-space sum over an axis is a dedicated logsumexp reduction.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The second operand b. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The elementwise stable log(exp(a) + exp(b)). logaddexp_() writes the result back into the receiver. Floating-point inputs only.

Gradient¶

logaddexp() is differentiable, with a backward that is a soft indicator of which operand dominated:

d/da logaddexp(a, b) = sigmoid(a - b) = exp(a) / (exp(a) + exp(b))
d/db logaddexp(a, b) = sigmoid(b - a)

The two gradients always sum to 1. When a far exceeds b, essentially all of the upstream sensitivity flows to a; at a == b it splits exactly 0.5 / 0.5.

Examples¶

Example 1. logaddexp(x, x) = x + log(2) for every element.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 3.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.logaddexp(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.6931, 1.6931, 3.3133]

The first two entries are 0 + log 2 and 1 + log 2. The third is 3 + log1p(exp(-1)) = 3.3133.

Example 2. The stability that motivates the method. The naive (a.exp() + b.exp()).log() overflows here; logaddexp() returns the right answer.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1000.0}).logaddexp(pluss::make_series({1000.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1000.6931]

Example 3. -inf behaves as “log of zero probability”. Two -inf operands combine to -inf with no NaN.

double ninf = -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({ninf}).logaddexp(pluss::make_series({ninf})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[-inf]

Example 4. The backward is sigmoid(a - b) and sigmoid(b - a), which sum to 1. Note the exact 0.5 / 0.5 split at the tie.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({2.0, 2.0, 1.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.logaddexp(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.26894142, 0.5, 0.88079708]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.73105858, 0.5, 0.11920292]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Use logaddexp() rather than (a.exp() + b.exp()).log() whenever the operands can be large. The naive form overflows and returns inf.

  • Floating-point inputs only; integer series are not promoted.

  • +inf in either operand makes the result +inf; two -inf operands give -inf; a NaN operand propagates.

  • For a log-space sum over a whole axis, reach for a reduction rather than chaining logaddexp() calls.

Summary¶

logaddexp(a, b) is a stable log(exp(a) + exp(b)):

  • broadcasts like add(); floating point only

  • built on the m + log1p(exp(-|a - b|)) shift so nothing overflows

  • differentiable, gradients sigmoid(a - b) and sigmoid(b - a) that sum to 1

See Also¶

  • Series::logaddexp2: the base-2 version.

  • Series::sigmoid: the function that the backward rule is.

  • Series::exp and Series::log1p: the stable pieces logaddexp() is assembled from.
